As of 6:55am CT this morning, Cassini is no more.

For the past 20 years, I've been tracking NASA's Cassini spacecraft. From her launch in 1997 to her demise this morning, Cassini explored our solar system on its cruise to Saturn, sending back valuable data. Once at Saturn, Cassini performed over a decade of science and carried the Huygens lander to Titan.

This morning, at about 6:52am CT, Cassini was just 3000 feet above Saturn's cloud tops, when she began to fire her stabilizing thrusters. Firing them hard to keep her antenna pointed to the Earth as her descent quickened, fighting to send every last bit of data she gathered as she was physically experiencing and interacting with Saturn's upper atmosphere. The atmosphere was warming and burning her skin, but she continued her fight.

Flight engineers on Earth announced her systems went into critical engine thrust mode. She was losing the battle. Pieces of her had melted or broken off. But with what was left of her, she stood her ground, kept her antenna pointed, and still told the people of Earth what she was experiencing, tasting, feeling, in Saturn.

At 6:55am CT, travelling at over 77,000mph, Cassini crashed into the clouds of Saturn, resulting in a loss of signal on all bands. Remote telemetry was sensed for another 45 seconds, and then there was nothing left of Cassini.

Goodbye old friend. Thanks for the science.
